note: Dante's Italian asks for "harsh and clucking rhymes", and the canto then supplies them: its rhyme words are full of hard, clashing consonants. The sound of the verse is made to fit the ugliness of the place.

quote: where all the weight of hell converges
note: The pit is the center of the earth. Every circle of rock above presses down on this one point.

The Italian is "a tongue that calls mamma and babbo", mummy and daddy. It is also a joke at his own expense: Dante is writing in Italian, the language of the nursery, not in the Latin thought proper to serious subjects.

context: A second call for help, after the one in Inferno 2. The bottom of Hell is the hardest thing he has yet had to describe.

note: A legendary musician and king. When he played his lyre, the stones came down from the mountain of their own accord and set themselves into the walls of his city. Dante asks for words with the same power to build.

context: The city of family slaughter is a fitting one to name at the edge of the ice. Its story returns at the end of this canto and in the next.

note: Animals have no immortal soul, so they cannot be damned. The words recall what Christ says of Judas: it would have been better for that man if he had never been born (Matthew 26:24).

context: At the end of Canto 31 he picked up Dante and Virgil in his hand and set them down on the floor of the pit.

note: The speaker is never identified. Since the voice speaks of "brothers", it may be one of the two brothers Dante is about to meet. Others take it as any soul in the ice, speaking of brothers in misery.

context: The ninth and last circle. Treachery is the worst sin in Dante's Hell because it destroys the trust and love that bind people together, so its punishment is cold, not fire: the traitors are fixed in ice, as far as possible from the warmth of God's love.

note: The Danube and the Don, the great river of Russia, stood for the frozen north, the coldest places a medieval Italian could think of.

Pietrapana is a peak of the Apuan Alps in northwest Tuscany, now called Pania della Croce. Tambernicchi has never been identified for certain. It may be Monte Tambura in the same range, or a mountain in the Balkans.

quote: when peasant girls dream of harvest time
note: Summer, when frogs croak through the warm nights. In the Italian the girl dreams of gleaning, picking up the grain left behind by the reapers. A homely picture of warmth, set against the ice.

quote: up to where shame would show
note: Up to the face, where a blush appears. The souls are sunk in the ice to the neck.
Storks make no call. They clatter their long bills together, and the souls' teeth make the same dry sound.
In this first zone the souls can bend their heads, so their tears fall away before they freeze. It is the one mercy of the ice, and it is taken away further in.

Napoleone and Alessandro degli Alberti, sons of Count Alberto of Mangona. They quarreled over their inheritance and over politics, and killed each other in the 1280s. The brothers who could not share their father's land now share one block of ice, still fighting.
A small river that runs down past Prato and joins the Arno just west of Florence. The Alberti held castles in its valley.

context: The speaker names the zone Dante is standing in. The souls so far have all killed members of their own families.

note: Mordred, who tried to seize King Arthur's throne. In the French romance of Arthur's death he is Arthur's son. In their last battle Arthur ran him through with a lance, and when it was pulled out, a ray of sunlight passed through the wound and broke his shadow on the ground.

The nickname of Vanni dei Cancellieri of Pistoia, who murdered a kinsman. The early commentators disagree about the details. The feud inside the Cancellieri family was blamed for dividing Pistoia, and then Florence, into the parties of the Blacks and the Whites.

A Florentine of the Toschi family. Early commentators say he murdered a young kinsman to get his inheritance, and was rolled through the streets in a barrel studded with nails and then beheaded. The story was so well known that any Tuscan would have heard it.

Alberto Camicione, of the Pazzi family of the upper Arno valley, who killed a kinsman named Ubertino. Almost nothing else is known of him. He is quick to name everyone around him: traitors in the ice betray each other still.

Carlino de' Pazzi, a relative who was still alive in 1300. In 1302 he would take a bribe to hand a castle full of Florentine exiles, his own party, over to their enemies. That is treason against one's side, punished in the next zone down, and beside it Camicione's crime will look small.
The center of the earth, which in medieval science was also the center of the universe. Everything heavy falls toward it. It is the furthest possible point from God.

quote: whether by will or fate or chance
note: Dante leaves open whether the kick was an accident, the working of God's justice, or his own doing. Given what he does to this soul next, the doubt seems deliberate.

context: The name gives the soul away. Dante suspects he has found the man whose treachery lost Florence the battle, and stops to make sure.
Without any marked border, the poets have walked from the first zone into the second. The souls named from here on betrayed their city or their party.

note: In the circles above, the damned often beg Dante to keep their memory alive on earth. The traitors want the opposite. To be remembered is to be remembered as a traitor, so Dante's offer is a threat.

quote: I grabbed him by the hair
note: The only time in the poem that Dante lays violent hands on a soul. Some readers see righteous anger at a traitor to Florence. Others see the cruelty of the ninth circle taking hold of the pilgrim himself.

context: After all his silence under torture, he is named by the traitor beside him. He takes revenge at once by naming that one and four more.

note: Buoso da Duera, a Ghibelline lord of Cremona. In 1265 he was posted to stop the French army of Charles of Anjou as it marched south to conquer the kingdom of Naples. He let it pass, and was believed to have been paid to do so: the "French silver".
In the Italian the sinners "stanno freschi", are kept cool: a grim understatement. The expression "stare fresco", to be in for trouble, is still used in Italian and is often traced to this line.

Tesauro dei Beccaria of Pavia, abbot of Vallombrosa and the pope's legate in Tuscany. In 1258 the Guelphs who ruled Florence accused him of plotting to bring back the exiled Ghibellines, and cut off his head.

context: Most of the traitors named in Antenora come from the wars of Dante's own Tuscany, where each party in turn drove the other into exile.

note: A Florentine nobleman of the Ghibelline party. In 1266, when the Ghibellines were losing their hold on the city, he went over to the popular rising against them and tried to make himself its leader.
The great traitor of the Song of Roland. He betrayed the rear guard of Charlemagne's army to the Saracens in the pass of Roncesvalles, where Roland and his companions were killed.
Tebaldello Zambrasi of Faenza. In 1280, to settle a private grudge against a Ghibelline family from Bologna that had taken refuge in his city, he opened a gate before dawn to their Guelph enemies.

quote: two souls frozen in one hole
note: Count Ugolino and Archbishop Ruggieri of Pisa, who are named, and whose story is told, at the start of the next canto.

One of the seven kings who attacked Thebes. In the Thebaid, the Latin epic by Statius, he is mortally wounded by the Theban Menalippus, kills him in return, and as he dies has the head brought to him and gnaws at it in rage.
